content.study:
Topic at a Glance
Article 246 of the Constitution of India is titled “Subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States”. It forms an integral component of Relations between the Union and the States (Articles 245–263), located within the “Centre–State” cluster. Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023.

Constitutional Text & Anatomy
(1) Notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3), Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “Union List”).

(2) Notwithstanding anything in clause (3), Parliament, and, subject to clause (1), the Legislature of any State 1 [omitted also, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List III in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “Concurrent List”).

(3) Subject to clauses (1) and (2), the Legislature of any State 1 [omitted has exclusive power to make laws for such State or any part thereof with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List II in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “State List”).

(4) Parliament has power to make laws with respect to any matter for any part of the territory of India not included in a State notwithstanding that such matter is a matter enumerated in the State List.

Constituent Assembly Intent & Doctrinal Foundation
The framers envisioned Article 246 as a fundamental structural instrument. In constitutional jurisprudence, every clause operates not in isolation but as part of an integrated, transformative organic document. Key aspect: Read with Article 246A for GST.

Procedural & Courtroom Anchors (Senior Counsel Checklist)
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing & Remedial Path: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.
4. Evidentiary Standards: Where disputed facts or legislative arbitrariness are alleged, evidentiary burdens under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA ss. 104–106) and official gazette notifications govern the record.

Key Statutory Ingredients to Establish
1. (1) Notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3), Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “Union List”).
2. (2) Notwithstanding anything in clause (3), Parliament, and, subject to clause (1), the Legislature of any State 1 [omitted also, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List III in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “Concurrent List”).
3. (3) Subject to clauses (1) and (2), the Legislature of any State 1 [omitted has exclusive power to make laws for such State or any part thereof with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List II in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “State List”).
4. (4) Parliament has power to make laws with respect to any matter for any part of the territory of India not included in a State notwithstanding that such matter is a matter enumerated in the State List.

Judicial Interpretation & Binding Ratios
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.

Current-Law Position & Milestone
Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. Any attempt by subordinate legislation or executive notifications to abridge the mandate of Article 246 is subject to judicial review under Articles 226 and 32.

hypotheticals.question: Examine the constitutional validity of the impugned directive in light of Article 246 and settled Supreme Court jurisprudence. What relief, if any, can be granted?
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. Scrutinize the constitutional source of power: Does Article 246 grant plenary power, or is it conditioned by express safeguards, legislative competence, or fundamental rights?
2. Apply the doctrine of ultra vires and manifest arbitrariness: If the directive creates arbitrary exceptions or bypasses statutory provisions, it violates Article 14 and the mandate of Article 246.
3. Examine procedural compliance: Substantive and procedural requirements under the Constitution cannot be waived on mere grounds of administrative convenience.
4. Balance public interest vs constitutional discipline: Constitutional limitations always prevail over executive fiat.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Case Brief & Legal Assessment: Scope and Application of Article 246 (Subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & CONSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT
Whether the State action, statutory enactment, or individual claim conforms to the constitutional mandate, procedural prerequisites, and substantive protections enshrined in Article 246 (Subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States) of the Constitution of India.

II. RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
Article 246 is situated in Relations between the Union and the States (Articles 245–263), governing the “Centre–State” dimension of Indian constitutional law.
The essential constitutional ingredients are:
1. (1) Notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3), Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “Union List”).
2. (2) Notwithstanding anything in clause (3), Parliament, and, subject to clause (1), the Legislature of any State 1 [omitted also, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List III in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “Concurrent List”).
3. (3) Subject to clauses (1) and (2), the Legislature of any State 1 [omitted has exclusive power to make laws for such State or any part thereof with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List II in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “State List”).
4. (4) Parliament has power to make laws with respect to any matter for any part of the territory of India not included in a State notwithstanding that such matter is a matter enumerated in the State List.

III. PROCEDURAL ANCHOR & REMEDIAL FORUM
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.

IV. JUDICIAL INTERPRETATION & AUTHORITY
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Supreme Court established that The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
Furthermore, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court reaffirmed that constitutional guarantees are justiciable and binding upon all state functionaries.

V. APPLICATION TO FACT PATTERNS
To apply Article 246:
1. Verify whether the impugned measure falls within the scope of the article's textual command.
2. Check whether any express exceptions, provisos, or constitutional limitations apply.
3. Subject the measure to tests of proportionality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14. If an ingredient is missing or breached, the measure is unconstitutional.

VI. CONCLUSION
Article 246 stands as a vital constitutional checkpoint. Any state action in breach thereof is void and amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION & CONSTITUTIONAL PHILOSOPHY
Article 246 of the Constitution of India, titled “Subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States”, represents a critical cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. Situated within Relations between the Union and the States (Articles 245–263), the provision balances state power with individual liberties and institutional accountability. The Constituent Assembly intended this provision to be an active, living guarantee rather than an ornamental declaration.
II. STATUTORY & DOCTRINAL DECONSTRUCTION
A forensic analysis of Article 246 reveals the following distinct constitutional limbs:
(a) Limb 1: (1) Notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3), Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “Union List”).
(a) Limb 2: (2) Notwithstanding anything in clause (3), Parliament, and, subject to clause (1), the Legislature of any State 1 [omitted also, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List III in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “Concurrent List”).
(a) Limb 3: (3) Subject to clauses (1) and (2), the Legislature of any State 1 [omitted has exclusive power to make laws for such State or any part thereof with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List II in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “State List”).
(a) Limb 4: (4) Parliament has power to make laws with respect to any matter for any part of the territory of India not included in a State notwithstanding that such matter is a matter enumerated in the State List.
The Article must be read in conjunction with the foundational architecture of the Constitution:
1. Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances: No branch of government possesses untrammelled discretion.
2. Rule of Law & Non-Arbitrariness: Every exercise of authority under Article 246 must satisfy the basic standard of fairness and reasonableness.
3. Transformative Constitutionalism: The provision must be interpreted progressively to advance justice, liberty, and equality as pledged in the Preamble.
III. JURISPRUDENTIAL EVOLUTION & LEADING CASE LAW
The Supreme Court of India has deconstructed Article 246 across several seminal judgments:
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225:
   Ratio Decidendi: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625:
   Ratio Decidendi: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.
IV. PROCEDURAL ROADMAP & LITIGATION CHECKLIST (SENIOR COUNSEL REFERENCE)
When approaching the Court under or in respect of Article 246:
1. Forum Selection: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Pleading Essentials: The writ petition or plaint must specifically plead:
   (a) The exact constitutional authority or violation under Article 246;
   (b) The factual narrative establishing how each statutory ingredient is satisfied or infringed;
   (c) The absence of an effective alternative remedy, or justification under the Whirlpool Corporation exceptions (breach of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, or complete lack of jurisdiction).
3. Evidentiary Standard: Discharge of burden under BSA ss. 104–106 and production of certified records.
V. IRAC PROBLEM ANALYSIS (PRACTICE HYPOTHETICAL)
Fact Matrix: The State issues a notification encroaching upon the domain of Article 246 without satisfying statutory preconditions.
Issue: Does the executive notification violate the constitutional guarantees and procedures of Article 246?
Rule: Under Article 246, state action is strictly conditioned by constitutional provisions and cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
Application: The impugned notification fails because it circumvents the procedural safeguards and lacks rational nexus to the constitutional objective. Applying the proportionality test, the State has failed to adopt the least intrusive means.
Conclusion: The notification is unconstitutional and void ab initio. The appropriate writ of certiorari or mandamus shall issue.
VI. CRITICAL APPRAISAL & CURRENT-LAW MILESTONE
Article 246 remains a vibrant instrument of governance, current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. A robust democracy requires rigorous adherence to its letter and spirit to protect the citizen against executive overreach and legislative excesses.

enhancement.definition: Article 246 defines the subject-matter competence of Parliament and State Legislatures by distributing legislative powers across the three lists in the Seventh Schedule. It confers exclusive power on Parliament over List I (Union List), exclusive power on State Legislatures over List II (State List), and concurrent power over List III (Concurrent List), backed by non-obstante clauses establishing the constitutional principle of Federal Supremacy in cases of irreconcilable conflict.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Indian federalism embodies a centripetal balance with a strong Centre. Where legislative entries in different lists appear to overlap, the conflict is resolved not by mechanical boundary lines, but by examining the 'pith and substance' (true nature and character) of the impugned legislation; where genuine, irreconcilable conflict persists, federal supremacy ensures Union predominance.

essentialIngredients: List I (Union List - Clause 1): Exclusive power of Parliament to make laws with respect to any matter in List I (defence, foreign affairs, atomic energy, banking, railways, interstate trade). Introduced with a non-obstante clause ('Notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3)').

List II (State List - Clause 3): Exclusive power of State Legislatures to make laws for the State with respect to any matter in List II (public order, police, public health, agriculture, local government). Subordinated by 'Subject to clauses (1) and (2)'.

List III (Concurrent List - Clause 2): Concurrent power of Parliament and State Legislatures (criminal law, civil procedure, marriage, contracts, transfer of property, economic planning). Subordinated to Clause (1) by 'Notwithstanding anything in clause (3), but subject to clause (1)'.

Union Territories Competence (Clause 4): Parliament has plenary power to make laws with respect to ANY matter (including State List matters) for Union Territories or territories not included in a State.

Doctrine of Pith and Substance: In case of incidental encroachment into another list, the court ascertains the dominant purpose and character of the law; if it falls substantially within competence, incidental encroachment does not invalidate it.
Federal Supremacy Rule: If an inevitable and irreconcilable conflict arises between List I and List II/III, List I prevails.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Article 246 is the legislative engine of Indian federalism, borrowing the three-list model from Section 100 of the Government of India Act, 1935.

### 1. The Hierarchy of Non-Obstante Clauses
The opening phrases of Article 246 establish a clear hierarchy of federal supremacy:
- Clause (1) begins: *'Notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3)'* — giving List I absolute priority over Lists II and III.
- Clause (2) begins: *'Notwithstanding anything in clause (3), but subject to clause (1)'* — giving Concurrent List priority over State List, but subordinating it to Union List.
- Clause (3) begins: *'Subject to clauses (1) and (2)'* — making State List subordinate to both Union and Concurrent Lists.
However, in *In re Central Provinces and Berar Act (1939)* and *State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)*, the courts established that federal supremacy is a **measure of last resort**; courts must first make every effort to read the entries harmoniously.

### 2. The Doctrine of Pith and Substance
Legislative entries are not powers, but fields of legislation that must be construed broadly and generously (*Navinchandra Mafatlal*). When a statute enacted under one list incidentally touches upon a subject in another list, the court applies the **Doctrine of Pith and Substance**:
- **Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce (1947):** The Bengal Moneylenders Act, 1940 enacted under State List ('moneylending') limited interest on promissory notes ('banking' and 'negotiable instruments' under Union List). The Privy Council held that the true nature and character (pith and substance) of the Act was moneylending; incidental encroachment on negotiable instruments did not invalidate it.
- **State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951):** The Bombay Prohibition Act (State List 'intoxicating liquors') incidentally affected the import of liquor (Union List). The Supreme Court upheld the Act, ruling that its pith and substance was total prohibition within the State.

### 3. Goods and Services Tax (Article 246A)
The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 inserted **Article 246A**, introducing a revolutionary constitutional departure from the exclusive compartmentalization of Article 246. Article 246A confers **simultaneous, concurrent legislative power** on both Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws with respect to Goods and Services Tax, guided by the cooperative federalism of the GST Council (Article 279A).
examples: Incidental Encroachment in Prohibition Law: A State Legislature enacts a law strictly banning the manufacturing, possession, and sale of liquor under Entry 8 of the State List. An alcohol importer argues that the law interferes with interstate import under Entry 41 of the Union List. Applying F.N. Balsara, the Supreme Court upholds the State law under the Doctrine of Pith and Substance, holding that its true nature is public health and prohibition, and the impact on imports is merely incidental.

Residuary Power over New Technology: Parliament enacts a comprehensive statute regulating artificial intelligence, cryptographic blockchain assets, and space mining. Because none of these subjects existed in 1950 or are enumerated in Lists II or III, Parliament validly exercises plenary residuary power under Article 248 read with Entry 97 of List I.
distinctions: Article 246 vs Article 248: Article 246 distributes enumerated subject-matter across the three lists of the Seventh Schedule; Article 248 vests exclusive residuary legislative competence in Parliament over any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent or State Lists.

Pith and Substance vs Colorable Legislation: Pith and substance asks 'What is the true nature and subject-matter of the statute?'; Colorable legislation asks 'Is the legislature disguisedly doing indirectly what it is constitutionally forbidden from doing directly?'
problemApplication: Issue: A State Legislature enacts the 'Moneylenders Debt Relief Act' under Entry 30 of the State List ('Moneylending and moneylenders'). Section 10 of the Act states that banks licensed by the Reserve Bank of India shall not charge more than 6% interest on agricultural loans. A nationalized bank challenges Section 10, arguing that banking is an exclusive Union subject under Entry 45 of List I. Is Section 10 constitutionally valid?

Rule: While a State can regulate private moneylenders under Entry 30 of List II, regulation of banking corporations is an exclusive Union subject under Entry 45 of List I. Where a state statute directly regulates the core banking operations of nationalized banks, it transgresses incidental encroachment and violates Article 246(1).

Application: Entry 45 of List I exclusively vests 'Banking' in Parliament. Dictating lending rates for nationalized banks directly trenches on the core domain of Central banking regulation under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and RBI Act, 1934.
Counterargument: The State asserts pith and substance in relieving indebted farmers under agricultural welfare.

Conclusion: Applying State of Gujarat v. Shri Ambica Mills, the direct regulation of commercial banks exceeds permissible incidental encroachment and is ultra vires Article 246(1) for invading the exclusive Union List.
